d.title: A failed statement inside a transaction leaves a decision to make
d.caption: **The second INSERT violates the primary key, the driver raises, and now the transaction is open with one statement applied and one failed.** Whichever branch you take must be explicit: without a ROLLBACK the first row stays pending, and a connection returned to a pool mid-transaction carries that state to the next request. **The real point is the except clause, not the BEGIN** — code that opens a transaction and has no rollback path is code that half-applies changes the first time anything goes wrong. A context manager does both ends for you, which is why it is the form to default to.

d.title: Four operational patterns, and the failure each one is there to prevent
d.caption: **Each row is one line of setup against one class of incident.** The pool cap is the one people set too high: a pool larger than the server's connection limit does not increase throughput, it converts a traffic spike into a refused connection for everybody. **And the timeout belongs on the server, not only in the client** — a client-side timeout stops you waiting and leaves the query running, still holding its connection and its locks. The retry has two preconditions that are easy to skip: only on transient error classes, and only for work that is idempotent.

d.title: Strictly less than, because the checkout event is the order
d.caption: **Every join condition in this feature table says strictly before the order's timestamp, and the measurement shows why.** For order 108 three events precede it and two do not — and one of those two is the checkout event, which carries the order's own timestamp. **Admit it and the feature “events in the last 7 days” contains the event that happened because the order happened**, which is a leak that looks like a brilliant feature in training and predicts nothing in production. The same cut-off discipline applies to prior orders, prior spend and days since last.

d.title: Three samples, and only one of them is reproducible anywhere
d.caption: **A seeded random is reproducible within one engine and one session, and nowhere else** — the draw depends on row order and row count, so it changes the day a row is inserted and differs between engines. That is fine for a one-off look and wrong for a train/test split somebody must reproduce. **The hash-of-the-key method is the one that survives everything:** the same key always lands in the same bucket, on any engine, however the table grows. Stratifying is a different concern — row-number within each stratum — and TABLESAMPLE samples pages rather than rows, so it is fast and only approximately proportional.

d.title: Three interview questions whose whole difficulty is the edge case
d.caption: **In each one the obvious query is right and the follow-up is about the row that is missing from it.** The inner self-join correctly excludes the CEO, whose manager is NULL — and the interviewer's next question is how to include them, which is a LEFT JOIN. **The anti-join has the trap worth saying out loud: NOT IN against a nullable column returns nothing at all**, which is lesson 1.2 arriving in an interview. Say which spelling you are using and why, because the reason is the answer they are listening for.

d.title: Consecutive dates and consecutive row numbers advance together
d.caption: **That is the entire gaps-and-islands trick: subtract the row number from the date and the result is constant inside a streak**, so grouping by that constant gives one group per streak. Nothing else in SQL does this as cheaply, and the same shape answers consecutive logins, sessionisation and uptime runs. **The DISTINCT on the first line is not tidiness — it is load-bearing:** a duplicate login on one date advances the row number without advancing the date, which breaks the arithmetic and splits one streak into two.

d.title: Four shapes that answer most reporting questions
d.caption: **Conditional aggregation is the one to internalise: a FILTER clause, or a CASE inside a SUM, pivots rows into columns without any pivot syntax** — and it is portable to every engine, which the dedicated PIVOT keywords are not. Median has a portable spelling and a short native one, and knowing both is the point: the native function is clearer where it exists. **And the last row is the shape people reach for a self-join to do** — first and last value per group, in one row, from two window functions rather than two joins.
